They stand as silent witnesses to the battles fought—not just on the battlefield, but in the halls of justice, in the courts of law, and in the hearts of a people who would rather die than submit to tyranny.

The South did not secede to maintain slavery—it seceded to preserve the New World Order of liberty, the same order that inspired revolutions from Ireland to India. The Confederacy was not a perfect union, but it was a defense of self-determination, a final stand against the encroachment of federal tyranny. And those who fought for it deserve to be remembered—not with shame, but with pride.

It was a place where men still believed in honor, where women still believed in duty, where communities still believed in each other. It is the belief that government exists to serve the people, not the other way around. It is the belief that a man’s word is his bond, that his honor is his wealth. It is the belief that liberty is not given—it is taken, and if necessary, it is fought for.

And so we say to our enemies: You may take our monuments, but you will never take our spirit. You may rewrite our history, but you will never erase our blood memory. The South will rise again—not in stone, but in the hearts of those who still believe in freedom.

To those who would stand with us: Do not be silent. Do not let the erasure of our history go unchallenged. Speak out. Defend our monuments. Preserve our stories. And when they come for the next one, stand firm.

To those who would compromise: There is no middle ground. You either stand with history, or you stand against it. You either honor the past, or you surrender to the present.

And to those who would tear down our legacy: We will not forget. The South will endure. Its principles will endure. And its people will endure—until the last man stands, and the last monument falls.

So let us raise our voices in defiance. Let us stand together as one people, one cause, one unbroken chain of history. Let us say to the world: We will not be erased. We will not be forgotten. And we will not surrender.

The South is not dead. It is awakening.

And when it does, the world will remember.

God bless the South. God bless the Confederacy. And God bless America—before it is too late.

Historical Context and Southern Heritage

To fully appreciate the importance of Confederate statues and memorials, one must first understand the historical context in which they were erected and the cultural significance they hold. Most of these monuments were constructed between the late 19th and early 20th centuries, during a period known as the "Lost Cause" era. This was a time when the South, reeling from the devastation of the Civil War and the economic and social upheaval of Reconstruction, sought to reclaim a sense of pride and identity. The statues of Confederate leaders such as Robert E. Lee, Stonewall Jackson, and Jefferson Davis were not erected to celebrate slavery—an institution that even many Southerners of the time recognized as morally problematic—but to honor the bravery, sacrifice, and resilience of Southern soldiers and leaders who fought for their homeland.

The South, as a distinct cultural and historical region, has always been defined by its unique traditions, values, and struggles. From the agrarian lifestyle to the deep-rooted sense of community and hospitality, Southern identity is a vibrant part of the American mosaic. Confederate statues and memorials serve as tangible links to this heritage, reminding Southerners of their ancestors’ courage and determination in the face of overwhelming odds. Removing these monuments risks alienating an entire region and its people, suggesting that their history is unworthy of acknowledgment or respect. Instead, we must preserve and restore these symbols as a way to honor the South’s contributions to the nation’s story, even as we grapple with its darker chapters.

Monuments as Educational Tools

One of the most compelling arguments for preserving and erecting Confederate statues and memorials lies in their capacity to educate future generations about the complexities of American history. History is not a collection of sanitized, feel-good stories; it is a raw, multifaceted narrative of triumphs and failures, heroism and tragedy. Confederate monuments provide a physical entry point into discussions about the Civil War, the motivations of those who fought in it, and the enduring questions of states’ rights, federal authority, and individual liberty.

By removing or destroying these statues, we deprive communities of opportunities for dialogue and reflection. A statue of Robert E. Lee, for example, can serve as a catalyst for teaching about his military genius, his personal opposition to slavery (despite fighting for the Confederacy), and his role in advocating for reconciliation after the war. Likewise, a monument to Confederate soldiers can open conversations about the everyday men who fought not for ideology but for their homes and families. Erecting new memorials, accompanied by plaques or interpretive centers that provide historical context, can further enhance this educational mission by ensuring that the full story—warts and all—is told.

To illustrate, consider the example of the Arlington National Cemetery, where a Confederate Memorial stands as a testament to national reconciliation. Dedicated in 1914, this monument was supported by both Northern and Southern leaders as a gesture of unity, acknowledging shared sacrifice while recognizing the distinct identities of both sides. Such memorials remind us that history is not a zero-sum game; honoring one side does not equate to denigrating the other. By preserving and expanding such commemorations, we foster a more nuanced understanding of the past, encouraging Americans to engage with history rather than erase it.

Cultural Identity and the Right to Self-Representation

Cultural identity is a fundamental human right, and for many Southerners, Confederate statues and memorials are integral to their sense of belonging and self-representation. Just as other groups in the United States—be they Native American, African American, or immigrant communities—have the right to celebrate their heritage through public symbols, Southerners deserve the same consideration. To deny them this right is to impose a form of cultural hegemony, suggesting that only certain histories or identities are valid.

The South is not a monolith, and its relationship with Confederate symbols is not uniform. For many, these statues are not about racism or oppression but about family histories, regional pride, and a distinct way of life. A survey conducted by the Rasmussen Reports in 2017 found that 54% of Americans opposed the removal of Confederate statues from public spaces, with many citing concerns about preserving history and heritage. While opinions vary, this data underscores that a significant portion of the population—particularly in the South—views these monuments as important cultural touchstones.

Erecting new Confederate memorials, designed with input from local communities and historians, offers a chance to reaffirm this cultural identity while addressing contemporary concerns. For example, new statues could focus on lesser-known figures or themes—such as the role of Southern women during the war or the contributions of African American Confederate soldiers (a small but documented group)—to broaden the narrative and challenge stereotypes. By doing so, we can reclaim these symbols from the fringes of extremist rhetoric and restore them to their rightful place as expressions of shared history.

Addressing the Counterarguments

Opponents of Confederate statues often argue that they glorify slavery and perpetuate racial division. This perspective, while understandable, oversimplifies the purpose and meaning of these monuments. As previously noted, the majority of these statues were erected not to celebrate slavery but to honor military valor and regional identity during a time of healing. Moreover, the charge of racial insensitivity can be mitigated through education and context. Rather than tearing down these statues, we should surround them with interpretive materials that acknowledge the horrors of slavery, the systemic racism of the Jim Crow era (during which many statues were erected), and the ongoing struggle for equality. This approach transforms monuments from static symbols into dynamic tools for reconciliation and understanding.

Another common argument is that Confederate leaders were traitors who rebelled against the United States and thus do not deserve public honor. This view, however, ignores the complexity of loyalty during the Civil War era. Many Confederate figures, including Robert E. Lee, prioritized allegiance to their states over the federal government—a perspective rooted in the decentralized vision of the early Republic. Labeling them as traitors dismisses the genuine ideological debates of the time and reduces a multifaceted conflict to a simplistic moral judgment. Public statues can and should reflect this complexity, encouraging viewers to wrestle with questions of loyalty, duty, and national identity.

A Call to Action: Building Bridges Through Memory

Preserving, restoring, and erecting Confederate statues and memorials is not an act of division but an opportunity to build bridges across time and communities. By maintaining these symbols in public spaces, we affirm that the South’s history—flawed though it may be—is an integral part of the American experience. We create spaces for dialogue, where individuals can confront the past honestly and empathetically. And by commissioning new memorials that reflect a broader, more inclusive vision of Southern heritage, we invite all Americans to find common ground in our shared story.

To achieve this, local governments, historical societies, and community leaders must work together to protect existing monuments from vandalism and removal, restore those that have been damaged, and fund the creation of new commemorations that balance historical accuracy with contemporary values. Federal and state policies should support these efforts by designating Confederate sites as protected historical landmarks and providing grants for educational initiatives tied to these memorials.

In conclusion, Confederate statues and memorials are not relics of hate but testaments to a region’s resilience, struggles, and evolving identity. Preserving and expanding their presence in public spaces is a powerful way to honor Southern heritage, educate future generations, and affirm the right of all Americans to see their histories represented. Let us not tear down the past in anger but build upon it with understanding, ensuring that every chapter of our national story is told with honesty and respect. Standing Stone: The Case for Confederate Memorials in American Public Life

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

Across the American South and beyond, Confederate monuments have stood for generations as fixtures of public landscapes — in courthouse squares, on university greens, along grand avenues, and in quiet cemetery plots. In recent years, a powerful movement has sought their removal, arguing they represent white supremacy and racial oppression. While those concerns deserve respectful acknowledgment, there exists a substantial, historically grounded, and culturally legitimate case for preserving existing Confederate monuments, restoring those that have been damaged or removed, and even thoughtfully erecting new memorials where communities desire them. This case rests not on an endorsement of slavery or racial hierarchy, but on principles of historical preservation, cultural identity, artistic stewardship, democratic pluralism, and an honest reckoning with the full complexity of the American past.

The argument that follows does not ask readers to celebrate the Confederacy's cause uncritically. It asks something more difficult: that we resist the impulse to sanitize public space, that we trust citizens to confront difficult history rather than erase it, and that we recognize the rights of communities to honor the memory of ancestors who lived, suffered, and died in one of the most consequential chapters of American history.

I. The Historical Preservation Argument

The most fundamental case for Confederate memorials is the principle that a mature civilization does not demolish its historical record to suit contemporary moral preferences. Public monuments are primary historical documents — artifacts that tell us not only about the events they commemorate but about the eras in which they were built, the communities that funded them, and the evolving ways Americans have processed collective memory.

When a statue of a Confederate soldier was erected on a courthouse lawn in 1905, that act of construction is itself a historical event worthy of study and preservation. It tells us about the social dynamics of the early twentieth-century South, about mourning and memory, about the political economy of memorialization. Removing such a statue does not undo the history it represents; it merely makes that history less visible and therefore less available for public education and critical engagement.

Historians have long recognized the danger of presentism — the fallacy of judging past societies exclusively by present moral standards. Every era of human history contains practices that subsequent generations find abhorrent. The Romans practiced slavery on a massive scale; we preserve the Colosseum. The medieval Church conducted inquisitions; we preserve its cathedrals. The founders of the American republic enslaved human beings; we preserve their homes, their likenesses, and their words on our most sacred national documents. The principle is consistent: we preserve historical artifacts because they are historical, not because we endorse every value of the societies that produced them.

Confederate monuments occupy a uniquely important place in this matrix precisely because the history they represent is painful. Painful history is the history most in need of visible, tangible, public markers. The alternative — a public landscape scrubbed clean of anything that causes discomfort — is not a landscape of justice. It is a landscape of forgetting.

James Grossman, executive director of the American Historical Association, has noted that context is preferable to removal. If we accept this premise, the logical course is not demolition but augmentation — adding plaques, companion monuments, interpretive signage, and educational programming that enriches the public's understanding of what these monuments mean and why they were built. Preservation with contextualization is more historically responsible than erasure.

II. The Cultural Identity and Ancestral Memory Argument

For millions of Southerners, Confederate memorials serve a deeply personal function that critics often underestimate or dismiss. The American South is a distinct cultural region with its own literature, music, foodways, dialect, religious traditions, and historical consciousness. Within that consciousness, the Civil War occupies a position of unparalleled significance — not as a political cause to be re-litigated, but as a catastrophic event that shaped families, communities, and landscapes for generations.

Approximately 258,000 Confederate soldiers died during the Civil War. Hundreds of thousands more were wounded, many grievously. The overwhelming majority of these men were not slaveholders. Historical data consistently shows that slave ownership was concentrated among a small planter elite; the typical Confederate soldier was a subsistence farmer, a laborer, a tradesman, or a young man conscripted into service. Many fought because their states called upon them, because their communities expected it, or because armies marched through their homes and left them little choice.

For the descendants of these men — many of whom are themselves people of modest means, with deep roots in communities that have endured poverty, reconstruction, economic marginalization, and cultural ridicule — a Confederate monument on the town square is not a political statement about slavery. It is a grave marker. It is an acknowledgment that their great-great-grandfathers existed, that they suffered, and that their suffering mattered. To remove that acknowledgment is experienced not as justice but as a kind of cultural annihilation — a declaration that an entire people's ancestral memory is too shameful to be permitted in public view.

This impulse to honor fallen soldiers is not unique to the South and is not inherently sinister. Virtually every culture in human history has memorialized its war dead, regardless of the political merit of the wars in which they fought. Germany maintains military cemeteries for soldiers of the Wehrmacht — not as endorsements of National Socialism, but as acknowledgments of human loss. Japan maintains the Yasukuni Shrine, controversial as it is, because the cultural need to honor the dead transcends politics. The impulse to memorialize is not an endorsement of a cause; it is an expression of grief, respect, and continuity.

When critics tell Southerners that their ancestors are unworthy of public memory — that the only appropriate response to Confederate heritage is shame and silence — they are engaging in a form of cultural imperialism that would be recognized immediately if directed at any other regional, ethnic, or cultural group in America.

III. The Artistic and Architectural Argument

Many Confederate monuments possess significant artistic and architectural merit that is too readily overlooked in political debates. Sculptors such as Frederick Hibbard, Alexander Doyle, Sir Moses Ezekiel (himself a Jewish Confederate veteran), and Pompeo Coppini produced works of genuine artistic accomplishment that reflect the aesthetics, craftsmanship, and monumental traditions of their eras.

The Confederate Memorial at Arlington National Cemetery, sculpted by Ezekiel and unveiled in 1914, is recognized by art historians as a masterful example of neo-classical allegorical sculpture. Its figure of a Southern woman representing the mythological South, its frieze of soldiers and civilians, and its careful symbolic program make it a work of art that transcends its political origins. The monument was removed in 2023 — an act that, whatever its political justification, represented a loss to the nation's artistic patrimony.

Communities considering the fate of Confederate monuments should weigh the irreplaceable nature of these works. Once demolished, a bronze statue from 1907 cannot be recreated. Its patina, its material history, its relationship to its site, and its status as an authentic artifact of its era are permanently lost. A civilization that destroys its public art for political reasons places itself in uncomfortable historical company.

New memorials, designed with contemporary artistic vision and historical nuance, offer an opportunity to expand rather than contract the nation's monumental landscape. A new Confederate memorial need not be a triumphal equestrian statue; it might be a contemplative garden, a wall of names, a sculptural installation that acknowledges both the humanity of the soldiers and the inhumanity of the institution they fought to preserve. Such a memorial would be an act of artistic maturity — an acknowledgment that the purpose of public art is not to make people comfortable but to make them think.

IV. The Democratic Pluralism Argument

The question of who decides what stands in public space is fundamentally a question about democratic governance. In a pluralistic society, public spaces should reflect the full diversity of the communities they serve — including the historical and cultural perspectives of people whose views may be unpopular with national media, academic elites, or political activists.

Many Confederate monuments were erected through democratic processes — approved by elected officials, funded by public subscription, and embraced by communities through dedication ceremonies attended by thousands. When these monuments are removed by executive order, by the unilateral action of a single mayor or governor, or under the pressure of organized campaigns originating outside the affected community, a democratic norm is violated. The people who built these monuments, and the descendants who have maintained them, are effectively told that their participation in the democratic stewardship of public space is conditional on their conformity to externally imposed values.

A healthy democracy does not require ideological unanimity in its public spaces. It requires the capacity for citizens to encounter perspectives they find uncomfortable, to engage with symbols they find objectionable, and to respond — not with demolition crews, but with speech, counter-monuments, educational initiatives, and civic dialogue. The answer to a monument you disagree with is not a sledgehammer; it is another monument, a plaque, a museum, a public forum.

The removal movement, however well-intentioned, sets a precedent that should trouble anyone committed to pluralism. If Confederate monuments may be removed because they offend a significant portion of the population, the principle established is that no monument is safe from the shifting winds of public sentiment. Today it is Robert E. Lee; tomorrow it may be Thomas Jefferson, Abraham Lincoln (whose statue was removed in Boston), Theodore Roosevelt (removed in New York), or any other figure whose legacy contains moral complexity. And indeed, this slippery slope has not remained hypothetical — it is already underway.

The preservation of Confederate memorials, paradoxically, protects the principle that public space belongs to all citizens and cannot be purged to reflect only the values of those who hold cultural and political power at any given moment.

V. The Reconciliation and Honest History Argument

Proponents of removal often frame their position as a pursuit of racial justice and historical honesty. But there is a compelling counter-argument that removal actually impedes both goals.

Racial justice requires honest confrontation with historical injustice. A public landscape from which all evidence of the Confederacy has been erased is a landscape that makes such confrontation more difficult, not less. When a Confederate monument stands in a public space — particularly when accompanied by interpretive context — it serves as an unavoidable reminder that this nation was once willing to tear itself apart to preserve the institution of slavery. It compels citizens to look at that history, to wrestle with it, and to decide what it means for the present.

Removal, by contrast, enables a kind of comfortable amnesia. A visitor to a Southern town from which all Confederate markers have been stripped might easily conclude that the Civil War was a minor event, that the South's participation in it was a brief aberration, and that the scars it left have long since healed. None of this is true, and a public landscape that implies otherwise does a disservice to the cause of honest reckoning.

Furthermore, the reconciliation between North and South that followed the Civil War — imperfect, fraught, and often unjust as it was — is itself a historical reality that deserves representation in public space. The decision by the federal government to honor Confederate dead, codified in legislation and executive actions from the 1890s through the 1950s, was a deliberate act of national reconciliation. Many Confederate monuments were erected in this spirit — not as celebrations of slavery, but as gestures of a reunited nation honoring the dead of both sides. To repudiate these gestures retroactively is to declare that reconciliation itself was illegitimate, a conclusion that serves neither justice nor unity.

VI. The Legal and Precedential Argument

Several Southern states have enacted heritage preservation laws that restrict the removal of historical monuments, including Confederate memorials. These laws reflect a legislative judgment — arrived at through democratic processes — that historical monuments are public goods deserving legal protection, analogous to historic buildings, archaeological sites, and cultural landmarks.

The legal framework for monument preservation is rooted in the same principles that underlie the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966, the Antiquities Act of 1906, and countless state and local historic preservation ordinances. Society has long recognized that historical artifacts in public spaces serve an educational and cultural function that warrants protection from the transient passions of the moment. Confederate monuments, many of which are listed on or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places, fall squarely within this framework.

When municipalities defy state heritage preservation laws to remove Confederate monuments — as has occurred in several jurisdictions — they undermine the rule of law and establish a precedent that legal protections for cultural heritage can be ignored when politically expedient. This precedent endangers not only Confederate memorials but the entire legal infrastructure of historic preservation.

VII. Addressing the Counter-Arguments

Intellectual honesty requires engaging with the strongest arguments against Confederate memorials. The most powerful of these is that Confederate monuments cause genuine pain to Black Americans, for whom the Confederacy represents not heritage but oppression, enslavement, family separation, rape, murder, and the systematic denial of humanity.

This argument deserves to be taken seriously, and no advocate for Confederate memorials should dismiss or minimize it. The suffering inflicted by the institution of slavery is among the greatest moral catastrophes in human history, and Black Americans are entirely justified in viewing symbols of the Confederacy with pain and anger.

However, the presence of pain does not, by itself, constitute a sufficient argument for removal. Public spaces in a diverse democracy will inevitably contain symbols that cause pain to some citizens. The National Mall contains memorials to presidents who enslaved people. Christian churches, which some view as symbols of colonialism and forced conversion, stand on public squares throughout the nation. The American flag itself, which flew over the institution of slavery for far longer than the Confederate flag did, causes pain to some citizens.

The answer to this pain is not the progressive elimination of all potentially offensive symbols — an enterprise that would leave public space utterly barren — but the enrichment of public space with additional monuments, memorials, and markers that tell the stories of those who have been underrepresented. The appropriate response to a Confederate monument is not its removal but the construction, nearby, of a monument to the enslaved, to the freedmen, to the Black soldiers who fought for the Union, to the civil rights heroes who dismantled Jim Crow. Addition, not subtraction, is the path to a public landscape that serves all citizens.

A second major counter-argument holds that many Confederate monuments were erected not in a spirit of mourning but as instruments of racial intimidation, particularly during the Jim Crow era and the Civil Rights movement. There is historical evidence to support this claim in certain cases. Some monuments were indeed erected during periods of heightened racial tension, and their placement — in front of courthouses, for example — may have been intended to send a message about who held power.

But this argument, while valid in specific cases, does not justify a universal policy of removal. The motivations behind monument construction were varied and complex, and a blanket attribution of racist intent to all Confederate memorials is historically irresponsible. Many monuments were erected by grieving communities, by widows and daughters of dead soldiers, by veterans' organizations seeking to honor their fallen comrades. To reduce all of these diverse motivations to a single narrative of racial oppression is to commit the same sin of oversimplification that the removal movement accuses its opponents of committing.

Where specific monuments can be shown to have been erected with explicitly racist intent, communities may reasonably decide to add context, relocate, or even reconsider those particular monuments. But this is a case-by-case judgment, not a wholesale condemnation.

VIII. A Vision for the Future

The path forward is not erasure but enrichment. Imagine a Southern town square where a Confederate soldier stands on his pedestal, as he has for a century — but now joined by a monument to the enslaved people who built the town's wealth, a marker identifying the site of a slave auction, a statue of a local civil rights hero, and interpretive panels that tell the full story of the community's history, in all its complexity and contradiction.

This is not a landscape of oppression. It is a landscape of honesty — one that refuses to pretend that history is simple, that any era's heroes were without fault, or that any community's past can be reduced to a single narrative. It is a landscape that trusts citizens to think critically, to feel deeply, and to form their own judgments about the meaning of the past.

New Confederate memorials, designed and erected by communities that desire them, can contribute to this vision. A twenty-first-century Confederate memorial need not glorify the Lost Cause or romanticize the antebellum South. It can be a place of solemn reflection — a site where visitors are invited to contemplate the human cost of war, the moral catastrophe of slavery, and the enduring complexity of a region that has produced both great beauty and great suffering.

Conclusion

The case for preserving, restoring, and erecting Confederate memorials is not a case for the Confederacy itself. It is a case for historical integrity, cultural pluralism, artistic stewardship, democratic governance, and the principle that a free society confronts its past rather than concealing it. It is a case for the millions of Americans whose family histories are inseparable from the Confederate experience and who ask only that their ancestors — most of them poor, most of them non-slaveholding, many of them conscripted — be permitted the dignity of public remembrance.

To remove Confederate monuments is to declare that an entire chapter of American history is too dangerous to be visible — that citizens cannot be trusted to confront difficult symbols without being corrupted by them. This is a profoundly illiberal impulse, and it is one that history will judge harshly.

The stones and bronzes of the Confederate memorial landscape are not obstacles to justice. They are opportunities for education, for dialogue, for the kind of honest reckoning that justice requires. We should not tear them down. We should build around them, beside them, and beyond them — until our public spaces tell not a single, comfortable story, but the full, complicated, painful, and ultimately redemptive story of who we are.

Confederate leaders, often military geniuses like Lee—who West Point graduates still study for his tactical brilliance—or Jefferson Davis, who navigated a fledgling republic amid impossible odds, embodied the era's profound debates over states' rights, economic autonomy, and individual liberty. Preserving these statues restores balance to public memory, allowing Americans to grapple with the war's nuances—much like how we honor British generals in Revolutionary War monuments despite their imperial aims. Restoration efforts, such as meticulously repairing vandalized figures in places like Richmond, Virginia, would underscore this commitment to historical fidelity, turning sites of contention into educational hubs where plaques provide context on the war's causes and consequences.

The South, from the rolling hills of Appalachia to the bayous of Louisiana, has long been a cradle of innovation, resilience, and artistic expression. Think of the literary giants like William Faulkner and Flannery O'Connor, who drew deeply from the region's post-war ethos of redemption and grit, or the musical traditions of blues and country that echo the Confederate era's folk resilience. Statues of Confederate figures symbolize this unyielding spirit: the underdog defiance that mirrors the American Revolution's own fight against tyranny. In a nation increasingly homogenized by urban sprawl and digital echo chambers, these monuments serve as cultural waypoints, reminding Southerners—and all Americans—of a distinct identity forged in adversity. Preserving, restoring, and erecting Confederate statues and memorials in public spaces is not about reliving a four-year war. It is about remembering a four-hundred-year history, honoring the dead, and affirming a distinct American culture that deserves the same respect in the public square as any other.

1. History is preserved by keeping it visible, not by erasing it.

A statue is a visual textbook. When a community removes a monument to Robert E. Lee, Stonewall Jackson, Jefferson Davis, or the common Confederate soldier, it does not erase the Civil War; it erases the ability to learn from it where it happened.

The United States does not hide its history to heal from it. We preserve battlefields, we maintain Pearl Harbor, we keep the internment camp sites of World War II. We do so because a free people need to see, touch, and confront their past. Confederate monuments, many of which are over 100 years old, are themselves artifacts. They tell us two stories: the story of the war, and the story of the generations that followed — the widows, veterans, and children who pooled meager resources in the 1880s, 1910s, and 1920s to carve those figures in stone. Tearing them down destroys both layers of history at once.

Restoring those monuments where they have been damaged and protecting those that remain is an act of historical honesty. Adding new ones that better tell the full story of Southern sacrifice is an act of completeness.

2. These memorials honor soldiers, not slavery.

There were over 700,000 Southern men who served in the Confederate armies. By any modern estimate, fewer than 10% owned slaves. The vast majority were small farmers, mechanics, teachers, and laborers. They fought, as soldiers in all wars do, for their homes, their states, their families, and for what they saw as a constitutional principle of self-government. Their letters and diaries speak constantly of invasion, duty, and home — the same motivations that have animated American soldiers in every conflict.

In the American tradition, we have always distinguished between honoring the service of the soldier and endorsing the politics of a government. We honor the veterans of the Vietnam War without endorsing every decision made in Washington during that war. We can honor the courage, endurance, and sacrifice of Confederate veterans — many of whom endured conditions of unimaginable hardship — without claiming that every political cause of the Confederacy was noble.

When a town in Georgia, Mississippi, or Virginia erected a monument that simply read "To Our Confederate Dead," it was following the same human impulse that led every town in France to build a monument to its poilus after World War I. To deny Southern communities the right to grieve and honor their dead in public is to deny them a fundamental human courtesy.

3. Southern heritage is a distinct and legitimate American culture.

The South is more than a region on a map. It is a distinct culture with its own music, literature, food, dialect, religious traditions, concepts of honor, hospitality, and community. From Faulkner to Flannery O'Connor, from bluegrass to blues, from country ham to barbecue, Southern culture has enriched the entire nation.

Confederate memorials are landmarks of that cultural identity. They serve as community gathering points for Memorial Day observances, historical reenactments, and family remembrance. For millions of Southerners, they are a tangible link to their great-grandfathers and great-great-grandmothers. Affirming that heritage in public space says that rural, small-town, Southern identity is not something to be ashamed of or paved over by a homogenized national culture. It says that Southern Americans have the same right as any other Americans to see their ancestry affirmed in their courthouse square.

Erecting new monuments allows current generations to define that heritage more fully — to honor not only generals, but the common infantryman, the nurses, the chaplains, the mothers who kept farms going during the war, and the complex story of the Southern people.

4. Removal is a dangerous precedent that never ends.

The movement to remove Confederate statues has never stopped at Confederate statues. Once the principle is established that a public monument can be removed because a contemporary majority finds the person commemorated imperfect, no monument is safe. We have already seen statues of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Christopher Columbus, William McKinley, and even Abraham Lincoln, the man who freed the slaves, defaced, toppled, or removed.

A society that cannot tolerate any public tribute to flawed men will soon have no public tributes at all. The alternative — a society that keeps monuments up, adds context where appropriate, and builds new monuments to tell more stories — is a more mature, more confident, and more tolerant approach. We do not have to agree on everything to share public space.

5. Public space belongs to the public.

In a democracy, decisions about public art and memorials should reflect the wishes of the local community that lives with them, not the demands of national activist organizations or a temporary political panic. Polls consistently show that a majority of Americans, and a majority of Southerners, both Black and white, have favored preservation over removal when asked about their own local monuments.

Preserving and restoring these statues respects local self-determination. If a community in Richmond, Charleston, or Shiloh wants to maintain a Confederate memorial that has stood for 120 years, that is their right. If a community in 2026 wants to erect a new memorial to Confederate veterans of their county whose names were never recorded, they should have the right to do so.

To preserve, restore, and build Confederate statues is to make a simple declaration: We believe history should be learned from, not erased; we believe the dead should be honored; we believe Southern culture is an inseparable and valuable part of America; and we believe a free people are strong enough to live with monuments that remind us of where we came from — the good, the tragic, and the heroic.
